Rapidly Progressive Glomerulonephritis (RPGN)

RPGN is a clinical syndrome of rapid (days-weeks) loss of renal function with extensive glomerular crescent formation on biopsy — "crescentic glomerulonephritis".

Pathogenesis — Three Immunological Types

  1. Type I — Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease (~10%)
    • Autoantibodies against the non-collagenous domain of α3 chain of type IV collagen (Goodpasture antigen) in GBM.
    • Linear IgG deposition on immunofluorescence.
    • Goodpasture syndrome — pulmonary haemorrhage + RPGN (anti-GBM also attacks alveolar basement membrane).
  2. Type II — Immune-complex mediated (~40%)
    • Post-infectious (post-streptococcal, endocarditis, staphylococcal), lupus nephritis, IgA nephropathy, membranoproliferative GN.
    • Granular ("lumpy-bumpy") immune-complex deposition on IF.
    • Underlying immune-complex disease drives crescent formation.
  3. Type III — Pauci-immune (~50%)
    • ANCA-associated vasculitides — granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener), microscopic polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss).
    • Little or no immunoglobulin on IF; antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCA anti-PR3, p-ANCA anti-MPO).
    • NETosis (neutrophil extracellular traps) releases PR3/MPO → triggers vasculitis & endothelial damage.
  4. Type IV — Double-antibody positive — both anti-GBM & ANCA positive; aggressive course.
  5. Type V — No antibodies — idiopathic.

Common Pathogenetic Pathway — Crescent Formation

  1. Glomerular capillary wall injury (immune-complex or antibody mediated) → endothelial & podocyte damage, capillary rupture.
  2. Fibrinogen and plasma proteins leak into Bowman's space → fibrin forms.
  3. Macrophages & T-cells infiltrate Bowman's space — parietal epithelial cells proliferate.
  4. Proliferating parietal epithelial cells + macrophages + fibrin = crescent — crescentic mass compresses & obliterates glomerular tuft → rapid loss of GFR.
  5. Within weeks — crescents become fibrous (collagen) → irreversible glomerulosclerosis.
flowchart TD A[Capillary wall injury: anti-GBM / IC / ANCA] --> B[Endothelial & podocyte damage] B --> C[Capillary rupture → fibrin leak into Bowman space] C --> D[Parietal epithelial cell proliferation] C --> E[Macrophage / T-cell infiltrate] D --> F[Crescent formation - cellular & fibrocellular] E --> F F --> G[Tuft compression → rapid GFR loss] F --> H[Fibrous crescent → glomerulosclerosis]

Clinical Features

Rapid oliguria / anuria, haematuria (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts), proteinuria, hypertension, oedema; anaemia (in ANCA / lupus), pulmonary haemorrhage (Goodpasture, ANCA vasculitis), sinusitis / nasal crusting (GPA), purpura / neuropathy (MPA).

Clinical Pearl

RPGN is a nephrological emergency — early diagnosis & aggressive immunosuppression (high-dose IV methylprednisolone + cyclophosphamide or rituximab + plasma exchange for anti-GBM) can salvage renal function. Delay of even days converts cellular (potentially reversible) crescents into fibrous (irreversible) ones.

Pathogenesis of Chronic Peptic Ulcer

An imbalance between aggressive (acid, pepsin) and protective (mucus, bicarbonate, mucosal blood flow, prostaglandins, growth factors) forces on gastroduodenal mucosa.

Major Factors

  1. Helicobacter pylori infection (most common — ~90% duodenal, 60-70% gastric)
    • Spiral, microaerophilic, urease-producing gram-negative bacterium colonises gastric mucus layer.
    • Urease → ammonia → alkaline microenvironment; protects organism & damages epithelium.
    • Vacuolating cytotoxin VacA → epithelial cell vacuolation & apoptosis.
    • Cytotoxin-associated antigen A (CagA) injected into epithelial cells via type IV secretion system → activates SHP-2, ERK, NF-κB → inflammation, hyperproliferation; CagA+ strains associated with gastric adenocarcinoma (1-6× risk) and ulcers.
    • Recruits neutrophils & T-cells → chronic active gastritis (antral — duodenal ulcer; pangastric / corpus — gastric ulcer & cancer).
    • Antral-predominant gastritis → ↑ gastrin → ↑ acid → duodenal gastric metaplasia → colonisation & duodenal ulceration.
  2. NSAIDs / Aspirin
    • Irreversible (aspirin) or reversible COX-1 inhibition → ↓ prostaglandin (PGE2, PGI2) synthesis.
    • ↓ Mucus & bicarbonate secretion, ↓ mucosal blood flow, ↓ epithelial proliferation, ↓ surface phospholipid → mucosal vulnerability to acid injury.
    • Direct topical injury (weak acids) — less important than systemic effect.
  3. Acid hypersecretion
    • Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma) — multiple, atypical, recurrent ulcers.
    • Antral G-cell hyperplasia; stress-related mucosal disease (Curling ulcer — burns; Cushing ulcer — head injury).
  4. Other risk factors
    • Smoking, alcohol, spicy food (irritants).
    • Stress — psychological, severe illness (ICU), surgery, trauma.
    • Genetic — family history, blood group O; HLA-DRB1*03, *04.
    • Other drugs — glucocorticoids (with NSAIDs), bisphosphonates, potassium chloride, SSRIs (with NSAIDs).
    • Crohn's disease, gastrinoma, viral (CMV, HSV), radiation, cocaine.

Pathological Sequence

  1. Mucosal injury → acute erosions (superficial, no scar).
  2. Continued injury → chronic ulcer — full-thickness loss of mucosa, extending into submucosa or muscularis propria.
  3. Ulcer floor — 4 zones: (1) superficial fibrinopurulent exudate with neutrophils; (2) fibrinoid necrosis; (3) granulation tissue with macrophages & proliferating capillaries; (4) fibrous scar at base.
  4. End arteries in muscularis may be eroded → haemorrhage; perforation → peritonitis.
  5. Healing — epithelial regeneration from edges; reconstitution of mucosa (submucosa & muscularis do not regenerate → scar); complications of healing — deformity (hour-glass stomach, pyloric stenosis).

Complications

Haemorrhage (haematemesis / melaena — most common), perforation (sudden severe pain, gas under diaphragm on X-ray), penetration (into pancreas — back pain; liver, colon), gastric outlet obstruction (pyloric stenosis — vomiting, succussion splash), recurrence, malignant transformation (gastric ulcer <1%; duodenal never), refractory healing.

Clinical Pearl

Test all peptic ulcer patients for H. pylori — urea breath test, stool antigen, or rapid urease test on biopsy. Triple therapy (PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin/metronidazole for 14 days) or quadruple (PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole) achieves 80-90% eradication; confirm eradication 4 weeks after completing therapy.

Serological Markers of Hepatitis B

Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a DNA virus (Hepadnaviridae) with multiple antigens — HBsAg (surface), HBcAg (core, intracellular, not usually detected), HBeAg (secreted e antigen, marker of infectivity). Antibodies develop in sequence.

MarkerSignificanceClinical Context
HBsAgSurface antigen — first marker; appears 1-10 weeks post-exposure (before symptoms)Acute & chronic infection; persistence >6 months = chronic carrier
Anti-HBsAntibody to surface antigen — protective, neutralisingRecovery from acute infection (after HBsAg clears); vaccination; HBIG passive immunisation
HBeAgSoluble e antigen — marker of active viral replication & high infectivityHigh viral load; high transmission risk (vertical, sexual, needle-stick)
Anti-HBeAntibody to e antigen — seroconversionLower infectivity; transition to inactive carrier state (except pre-core mutant — HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis)
HBcAgCore antigen — intracellular, not routinely detected in serum—
Anti-HBc IgMFirst antibody to appear; marker of acute infectionAcute hepatitis B; reactivation of chronic infection
Anti-HBc IgGPersists for life — past exposureChronic or resolved infection; differentiates from vaccine (vaccine recipients have only anti-HBs, no anti-HBc)
HBV DNA (PCR)Direct measure of viral loadDiagnosis (window period), monitoring therapy, mother-to-child transmission risk, pre-core / basal core promoter mutants (HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis)

Serological Patterns — Common Clinical Scenarios

  • Acute hepatitis B — HBsAg +, HBeAg +, anti-HBc IgM +, HBV DNA +, ALT high.
  • Resolved / natural immunity — HBsAg −, anti-HBs +, anti-HBc IgG +.
  • Vaccine immunity — HBsAg −, anti-HBs +, anti-HBc −.
  • Chronic active hepatitis (HBeAg +) — HBsAg + >6 months, HBeAg +, anti-HBc IgG +, HBV DNA high, ALT raised.
  • HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis (pre-core mutant) — HBsAg +, HBeAg −, anti-HBe +, HBV DNA high, ALT raised.
  • Inactive carrier — HBsAg + >6 months, anti-HBe +, HBV DNA low or undetectable, ALT normal.
  • Occult HBV infection — HBsAg −, anti-HBc + (± anti-HBs), HBV DNA low in liver / serum.
  • Window period — HBsAg cleared, anti-HBs not yet developed, only anti-HBc IgM +.

Clinical Pearl

All pregnant women should be screened for HBsAg; if positive, infant receives HBIG + vaccine within 12 h of birth and completes vaccination series — reduces vertical transmission from 90% to <5%. Patients with chronic HBV benefit from nucleos(t)ide analogues (tenofovir, entecavir) — high barrier to resistance & can be used long-term.

Hashimoto's Thyroiditis

Hashimoto thyroiditis (chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis) is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions — an organ-specific autoimmune disease with autoantibodies against thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) & thyroglobulin.

Etiopathogenesis

  • Genetic susceptibility — HLA-DR3, HLA-DR5, CTLA-4 polymorphisms; female : male 10:1; family history; associated with other autoimmune disease (type-1 DM, Addison, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo, Sjögren, SLE).
  • Immune mechanism — CD4+ T-helper cells (Th1) recognise thyroid antigen presented by HLA-DR → activate cytotoxic CD8+ T-cells that destroy thyrocytes; B-cells produce anti-TPO & anti-thyroglobulin antibodies.
  • Antibodies
    • Anti-TPO (microsomal) — 90-95% sensitive; blocks TPO action, fixes complement → thyroid cell damage.
    • Anti-thyroglobulin — 50-60%.
    • TSH-receptor blocking antibodies — cause atrophy & hypothyroidism in atrophic variant.
    • Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC).
  • Apoptosis — upregulated Fas-FasL on thyrocytes & infiltrating lymphocytes; loss of inhibitor of apoptosis.
  • Environmental triggers — high iodine intake, selenium deficiency, infections (Yersinia, HCV), interferon-α, radiation, certain drugs (amiodarone, lithium, cytokines).

Microscopic Features

  • Gross — diffuse, symmetric, firm, rubbery enlargement; lobulated; tan-yellow; capsule intact.
  • Microscopy
    • Dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with germinal centres.
    • Thyroid follicles small, with reduced colloid; colloid is eosinophilic & fragmented.
    • Hürthle (oxyphil, Askanazy) cells — follicular epithelial cells with abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm (packed with mitochondria); metaplastic change characteristic.
    • Variable fibrosis — more in late stage ("fibrous variant") — dense keloid-like fibrosis replaces thyroid.
    • Foci of squamous metaplasia.
    • Pauci-acute inflammation; plasma cells prominent.
  • Variant — Fibrous atrophic thyroiditis — small, atrophic gland with extensive fibrosis; presents with hypothyroidism without goitre; common in elderly women.
  • Variant — Juvenile Hashimoto — in children & adolescents; often initially hyperthyroid ("Hashitoxicosis"); less fibrosis.

Clinical Features

Painless, gradually enlarging goitre; symptoms of hypothyroidism (fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, menorrhagia, bradycardia, slow relaxation of reflexes). Some present with hyperthyroidism early (Hashitoxicosis). Risk of B-cell lymphoma (MALT) — long-standing Hashimoto is a predisposing condition.

Clinical Pearl

Anti-TPO is the single most useful antibody — present in >90% of cases. Fine-needle aspiration is rarely needed (clinical & serological diagnosis suffices). Treatment — levothyroxine replacement titrated to TSH; surgery only for compressive symptoms, suspicion of malignancy, or lymphoma.

Molecular Pathogenesis of Colorectal Carcinoma

Colorectal cancer (CRC) develops via the "adenoma-carcinoma sequence" — accumulation of multiple genetic & epigenetic alterations over 10-15 years. Three major molecular pathways have been identified.

1. Chromosomal Instability (CIN) Pathway — ~70% (APC/β-catenin)

  • APC loss (5q) — germline in familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), somatic in sporadic CRC. APC normally degrades β-catenin via GSK-3β; its loss → β-catenin accumulates → translocates to nucleus → binds Tcf-4 → transcription of c-MYC, cyclin D1 → proliferation. Earliest event — aberrant crypt foci → early adenoma.
  • KRAS mutation (12p) — activating point mutation in 40-50% of adenomas >1 cm — drives proliferation through MAPK pathway; not in small adenomas (suggests it drives progression from early to late adenoma).
  • SMAD2 / SMAD4 / DCC loss (18q) — loss of TGF-β signalling (growth inhibitory); drives progression to late adenoma.
  • p53 loss (17p) — in 70-80% of CRCs; loss of cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis, DNA repair → carcinoma.
  • Additional alterations — telomerase activation, angiogenesis (VEGF), invasion (MMPs).

2. Microsatellite Instability (MSI) Pathway — ~15% (Mismatch Repair Defect)

  • Defect in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes — MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 (also EPCAM).
  • Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) — germline MMR mutation, autosomal dominant; Amsterdam criteria; early-onset right-sided colon cancer, endometrial, ovarian, gastric, urinary tract cancers; lifetime CRC risk 60-80%.
  • Sporadic — MLH1 promoter hypermethylation (CIMP — CpG island methylator phenotype); BRAF V600E mutation distinguishes sporadic from Lynch.
  • Loss of MMR → accumulation of mutations in microsatellites (short repetitive sequences); especially in genes with microsatellites in coding region — TGFβRII, BAX, IGF2R.
  • Clinical — high-frequency MSI (MSI-H) tumours have better prognosis & respond to immune-checkpoint inhibitors (PD-1 blockade).

3. Serrated Pathway — ~15%

  • Begins in serrated polyps — hyperplastic polyps, sessile serrated adenomas (SSA/P), traditional serrated adenomas.
  • Activating BRAF V600E mutation → MAPK pathway → proliferation.
  • CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP) → silencing of MLH1 → MSI-H.
  • Right colon predominance; mucinous, poorly differentiated histology; poor prognosis if MSS.
flowchart TD A[Normal epithelium] --> B[APC loss → aberrant crypt foci] B --> C[KRAS mutation → early adenoma] C --> D[SMAD2/4, DCC loss → late adenoma] D --> E[p53 loss → carcinoma] F[MMR defect MLH1, MSH2] --> G[Microsatellite instability] G --> H[Right-sided, mucinous, Lynch syndrome CRC] I[BRAF mutation + CIMP] --> J[Sessile serrated adenoma] J --> K[CIMP-high + MLH1 methylation → MSI-H CRC]

Clinical Pearl

All CRCs should be tested for MMR (IHC for MLH1/MSH2/MSH6/PMS2) or MSI (PCR / NGS). Loss of MLH1 + BRAF mutation = sporadic; loss of MSH2/MSH6/PMS2 or MLH1 without BRAF = consider Lynch syndrome → germline testing. MSI-H tumours respond dramatically to pembrolizumab / nivolumab.

Emphysema — Pathogenesis & Types

Emphysema is a permanent enlargement of the airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole, accompanied by destruction of alveolar walls without obvious fibrosis.

Pathogenesis

  1. Protease-antiprotease imbalance
    • Neutrophils & macrophages release elastase, cathepsin G, proteinase 3, MMPs (especially MMP-9, MMP-12).
    • α1-antitrypsin (AAT) normally inhibits elastase; AAT deficiency (PiZZ phenotype) → unopposed elastase activity → alveolar wall destruction.
    • Oxidative stress (cigarette smoke) oxidises methionine-358 of AAT → functional AAT deficiency in smokers.
  2. Oxidative stress — cigarette smoke generates free radicals → lipid peroxidation, antiprotease inactivation, apoptosis of structural cells.
  3. Inflammation — neutrophils, macrophages, CD8+ T-cells infiltrate small airways; cytokines IL-8, TNF-α, leukotriene B4 amplify inflammation.
  4. Apoptosis / senescence — endothelial & alveolar epithelial cell apoptosis, reduced VEGF signalling, accelerated ageing (telomere shortening, SASP).
  5. α1-Antitrypsin deficiency — autosomal recessive, chromosome 14; PiZZ phenotype causes panacinar emphysema, especially lower lobes, in non-smokers by 4th-5th decade; misfolded protein accumulates in hepatocytes → liver disease.

Types of Emphysema (anatomical — within acinus)

TypeDistributionCause / Associations
Centriacinar (centrilobular)Proximal acinus (respiratory bronchioles); upper lobeSmoking — most common type
Panacinar (panlobular)Entire acinus uniformly; lower lobeα1-antitrypsin deficiency
Paraseptal (distal acinar)Distal acinus; subpleural & along septa; upper lobeSpontaneous pneumothorax in young adults; bullae formation
Irregular (paracicatricial)Around scars — TB, pneumoconiosis, infarctUsually asymptomatic; no airflow limitation
BullousLarge blebs >1 cmPneumothorax; surgical bullectomy
CompensatoryOverexpansion of remaining lungPost-resection or collapse
Senile (age-related)Mild uniform enlargementAgeing; no inflammation
InterstitialAir in interstitiumMechanical ventilation, trauma → pneumomediastinum

Clinical Features

Progressive dyspnoea, chronic cough, pursed-lip breathing, barrel chest, hyper-resonance, decreased breath sounds, weight loss, "pink puffer" phenotype.

Clinical Pearl

Centriacinar = smokers + upper lobes; Panacinar = AAT deficiency + lower lobes. Always check serum AAT level in young-onset COPD, basal-predominant emphysema, or family history of early-onset lung / liver disease. Augmentation therapy (weekly IV AAT) is indicated for confirmed deficiency with airflow obstruction.

Megaloblastic Anaemia — Blood & Marrow Findings

Megaloblastic anaemia results from impaired DNA synthesis (most commonly vitamin B12 or folate deficiency) → asynchronous nuclear-cytoplasmic maturation — nucleus lags behind cytoplasm (megaloblastic change). Affects all rapidly proliferating tissues — bone marrow, gut, mucosa.

Peripheral Blood Smear

  • Macrocytosis — MCV >100 fL (often 110-130 fL); oval macrocytes (large oval-shaped RBCs).
  • Anisocytosis, poikilocytosis — tear-drop cells, schistocytes.
  • Basophilic stippling, Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnants), Cabot rings, siderotic granules.
  • Hypersegmented neutrophils (≥5 lobes in >5% of neutrophils; classical & earliest finding).
  • Leukopenia, thrombocytopenia in advanced cases (pancytopenia may be present).
  • Reduced reticulocyte count for degree of anaemia (ineffective erythropoiesis).
  • Increased LDH, decreased haptoglobin (intramedullary haemolysis — "ineffective erythropoiesis").
  • Indirect bilirubin mildly raised.

Bone Marrow Findings

  • Hypercellular marrow — erythroid hyperplasia (M:E ratio reversed — 1:1 or 1:3).
  • Megaloblastic erythroid precursors — large cells with abundant basophilic cytoplasm but immature nuclear chromatin ("nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony"); nuclei show open, sieve-like chromatin.
  • Giant metamyelocytes & giant band forms — characteristic of granulocytic series.
  • Giant megakaryocytes with hyperlobulated nuclei.
  • Increased mitotic figures; karyorrhexis & nuclear fragmentation.
  • Iron stores increased; ringed sideroblasts may be seen.
  • hallmark — nuclear maturation lags cytoplasmic maturation in all lineages.

Distinguishing B12 vs Folate Deficiency

TestB12 DeficiencyFolate Deficiency
Serum B12Low (<200 pg/mL)Normal
Serum folateNormal or highLow (<3 ng/mL)
RBC folateNormalLow
Methylmalonic acidElevatedNormal
HomocysteineElevatedElevated
Neurological signsSubacute combined degeneration of cordAbsent

Clinical Pearl

Hypersegmented neutrophils are the earliest & most reliable peripheral clue. Always check B12 in elderly, strict vegetarians, post-gastrectomy, ileal disease, metformin users, and any patient with unexplained macrocytosis, pancytopenia, or neurological symptoms (subacute combined degeneration — loss of dorsal columns & lateral corticospinal tracts, peripheral neuropathy, cognitive impairment). Folate replacement alone in B12 deficiency can worsen neurological deficit.

WHO Classification of Testicular Tumours (2016)

CategorySubtypes
Germ cell tumours (~95%) Single histologic type:
• Seminoma
• Spermatocytic tumour (formerly spermatocytic seminoma)
• Embryonal carcinoma
• Yolk sac tumour (infantile embryonal carcinoma)
• Choriocarcinoma
• Teratoma (mature, immature, with malignant component)
Multiple types (mixed GCT — 60%): combination of above
Sex cord-stromal tumours (~4%)Leydig cell tumour, Sertoli cell tumour, granulosa cell tumour (adult & juvenile), thecoma-fibroma group, mixed & unclassified
Tumours of collecting ducts & reteAdenocarcinoma of rete testis
Miscellaneous nonspecific stromalSarcomas (liposarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma), lymphoma (most common testicular tumour in elderly), metastatic

Morphology of Seminoma

Seminoma is the most common pure germ cell tumour of the testis (~50% of GCTs); peak age 30-40 years (slightly older than non-seminomatous). Highly radiosensitive & chemosensitive; best prognosis among malignant GCTs.

Gross

  • Large, well-circumscribed, firm, homogeneous, grey-tan to pink, lobulated cut surface.
  • Bulges from capsule; usually replaces testicular parenchyma.
  • Often no haemorrhage or necrosis (in contrast to embryonal carcinoma); areas of necrosis may occur in large tumours.
  • Tunica albuginea usually intact.

Microscopy

  • Sheets, nests or cords of uniform large polygonal tumour cells with clear or granular eosinophilic cytoplasm; central round nuclei with prominent nucleoli; clear cytoplasm due to glycogen & lipid (PAS positive, diastase sensitive).
  • Cells separated by delicate fibrous septa containing lymphocytes (T-cells), plasma cells, occasional eosinophils.
  • Granulomatous reaction (epithelioid histiocytes & Langhans giant cells) in 50%.
  • Mitotic figures vary; syncytiotrophoblastic giant cells in 10-15% (may secrete low hCG — important for serum marker interpretation).
  • Necrosis & haemorrhage uncommon.
  • Immunohistochemistry — SALL4 (master germ cell marker), OCT3/4, PLAP (membranous), CD117 (c-KIT), D2-40 positive; CD30, AFP, hCG negative (except syncytiotrophoblasts).

Clinical Features

Painless testicular enlargement; firm mass; occasional dull ache or heaviness. Lymphatic spread — para-aortic (left) & interaortocaval / paracaval nodes (right) → mediastinal → supraclavicular. Haematogenous — lung. Serum markers — LDH raised; hCG mildly raised (if syncytiotrophoblasts); AFP normal (AFP elevation indicates non-seminomatous component).

Clinical Pearl

Seminoma is exquisitely radios- & chemosensitive — Stage I disease has >99% 5-year survival with orchiectomy ± single-cycle carboplatin or low-dose para-aortic radiotherapy. Advanced disease — BEP (bleomycin + etoposide + cisplatin) chemotherapy cures >85%. Spermatocytic tumour (separate entity, older men, indolent, no metastasis) — orchiectomy alone is curative.

Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia (CML)

CML is a myeloproliferative neoplasm arising from a pluripotent haematopoietic stem cell, characterised by uncontrolled proliferation of granulocytic precursors with the Philadelphia chromosome [t(9;22)(q34;q11.2)] producing the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene.

Pathophysiology

  • Reciprocal translocation between chromosome 9 (ABL gene) & chromosome 22 (BCR gene) → BCR-ABL1 fusion oncoprotein with constitutive tyrosine kinase activity.
  • BCR-ABL1 activates multiple downstream pathways — RAS-MAPK, JAK-STAT, PI3K-AKT — driving proliferation, inhibiting apoptosis, reducing adhesion to bone marrow stroma (cells escape into blood).
  • P210 fusion protein in classic adult CML; P190 in Ph+ ALL; P230 in rare neutrophilic CML.
  • Three clinical phases — chronic (3-5 yr), accelerated (3-9 mo), blast crisis (acute leukaemia — AML 70% / ALL 30%; median survival 3-6 mo without treatment).

Clinical Features

  • Peak age 40-60 yr; male : female 1.5:1.
  • Symptoms — fatigue, weight loss, night sweats, low-grade fever, early satiety, left upper quadrant fullness/pain (splenic infarction), gout (hyperuricaemia).
  • Signs — splenomegaly (90%, often massive), hepatomegaly, pallor, bruising, priapism (in young men — leucostasis), retinal haemorrhages, sweet syndrome.
  • Asymptomatic — incidental finding of high WBC on routine CBC.

Laboratory Findings

  • CBC — marked leukocytosis (WBC 50,000-300,000/μL); anaemia; thrombocytosis (often >600,000/μL); basophilia (cardinal finding in any myeloproliferative neoplasm); eosinophilia.
  • Peripheral smear — full spectrum of granulocytic differentiation (myeloblasts <10%, promyelocytes, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, bands, neutrophils) — "left shift"; pseudo-Pelger-Huet cells; basophilia; eosinophilia; tear-drop cells occasional.
  • Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score — markedly low (distinguishes from leukemoid reaction — high LAP).
  • Bone marrow — hypercellular, marked granulocytic hyperplasia (M:E >10:1); megakaryocytic hyperplasia with dwarf megakaryocytes; reticulin fibrosis in advanced disease; sea-blue histiocytes; blast count low in chronic phase.
  • Cytogenetics — Philadelphia chromosome [t(9;22)] in >95%; FISH or RT-PCR for BCR-ABL1 transcript.
  • Biochemical — high serum uric acid, vitamin B12 (from transcobalamin I produced by granulocytes), LDH; low or low-normal LAP.
  • Phase definitions
    • Chronic phase — blasts <10% in blood & marrow.
    • Accelerated phase — blasts 10-19%, basophils >20%, platelets <100,000 or >1,000,000 unresponsive, spleen enlarging, new clonal cytogenetic abnormalities.
    • Blast crisis — blasts ≥20% in blood/marrow; extramedullary blast proliferation (chloroma).

Clinical Pearl

Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) — imatinib (first-generation), dasatinib & nilotinib (second-generation), bosutinib & ponatinib (later) — target BCR-ABL1 and have transformed CML. 10-year survival now >85% with daily oral TKI therapy. Monitor response by BCR-ABL1 transcript levels (qRT-PCR) — major molecular response (MMR = BCR-ABL1 ≤0.1% IS) is the goal; deep molecular response (DMR = MR4.5) allows consideration of treatment-free remission in select patients.

Haemolytic Anaemia — Definition & Classification

Haemolytic anaemia is anaemia resulting from premature destruction of red blood cells (RBC lifespan <120 days), with the rate of destruction exceeding bone marrow's compensatory capacity (which can increase erythropoiesis 6-8 fold).

Classification

A. By Site of Haemolysis

  1. Intravascular — RBC destruction within circulation; haemoglobinaemia, haemoglobinuria (black urine), haemosiderinuria, methaemalbuminaemia, low haptoglobin, raised LDH. Causes — ABO mismatch transfusion, PNH, malaria (blackwater fever), clostridial sepsis, severe burns, prosthetic valve, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (HUS, TTP, DIC, malignant hypertension), snake & spider venoms, marching haemoglobinuria.
  2. Extravascular — RBC destruction by macrophages of spleen (mainly) & liver; jaundice, splenomegaly, raised indirect bilirubin. Causes — most immune haemolytic anaemias, hereditary spherocytosis, sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, haemoglobinopathies.

B. By Inherited vs Acquired

InheritedAcquired
RBC membrane defects
Hereditary spherocytosis (ankyrin, spectrin, band 3 deficiency); hereditary elliptocytosis; hereditary stomatocytosis; hereditary pyropoikilocytosis; PNH (acquired)Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PIGA mutation)
RBC enzyme defects
G6PD deficiency; pyruvate kinase deficiency; hexokinase; pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase deficiency—
Haemoglobinopathies
Thalassaemias (α, β); sickle cell disease; HbC, HbD, HbE; unstable Hb—
Immune-mediated
—Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) — warm IgG (idiopathic, SLE, lymphoma, drugs); cold agglutinin disease (IgM, Mycoplasma, EBV); paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria (Donath-Landsteiner, syphilis); alloimmune — haemolytic transfusion reaction, haemolytic disease of newborn
Microangiopathic
—DIC, HUS, TTP, malignant hypertension, HELLP, prosthetic valves, severe burns, malignancy
Infections
—Malaria, babesiosis, Clostridium welchii, Bartonella, Leptospira
Drugs / toxins
—Oxidant drugs (in G6PD deficiency); dapsone, primaquine; snake/spider venom; copper (Wilson); lead; arsenic

General Lab Features of Haemolysis

  • Anaemia — normocytic normochromic (with high reticulocyte count → may appear macrocytic).
  • Reticulocytosis (>2%) — bone marrow compensation.
  • Raised indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin, raised LDH, low haptoglobin (intravascular).
  • Smear — polychromasia, spherocytes, schistocytes, sickle cells, target cells depending on cause.
  • Urine — haemoglobinuria, haemosiderinuria (intravascular).
  • Bone marrow — erythroid hyperplasia.

Clinical Pearl

Always check reticulocyte count first — low reticulocytes with haemolysis suggests aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19 in sickle cell / hereditary spherocytosis) or megaloblastic crisis (folate depletion). DAT (direct antiglobulin test) differentiates immune (positive) from non-immune causes.

Alcoholic Liver Disease (ALD)

ALD is a spectrum of hepatic pathology caused by chronic alcohol consumption — steatosis (fatty change) → alcoholic steatohepatitis (ASH) → progressive fibrosis → cirrhosis. Alcohol metabolism generates acetaldehyde & reactive oxygen species; women are more susceptible than men at lower doses (>20 g/day vs >40 g/day in men).

Morphological Changes

1. Hepatic Steatosis (Fatty Liver) — Earliest Reversible Stage

  • Gross — enlarged, yellow, greasy, soft liver with rounded edges; up to 2-3 kg.
  • Microscopy — macrovesicular steatosis (large lipid droplet displacing nucleus to periphery) predominantly in centrilobular (zone 3) hepatocytes; may be mixed microvesicular in severe cases.
  • Mild ballooning degeneration; no significant inflammation or fibrosis.

2. Alcoholic Steatohepatitis (ASH) — Alcoholic Hepatitis

  • Ballooning degeneration — hepatocytes swollen with clumped cytoplasm & eosinophilic Mallory-Denk bodies (tangled intermediate filaments — keratin 8/18 + ubiquitin + p62), often surrounded by neutrophils.
  • Necrosis of hepatocytes — particularly centrilobular (zone 3).
  • Megamitochondria — enlarged eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions.
  • Mallory-Denk bodies — classic but not pathognomonic (also seen in NASH, chronic cholestatic disorders, Wilson disease).
  • Neutrophilic infiltrate (rather than lymphocytic as in chronic viral hepatitis).
  • Foamy degeneration of hepatocytes; cholestasis may be present.
  • Sinusoidal fibrosis — pericellular & perivenular ("chicken-wire" fibrosis; collagen deposition around hepatocytes in zone 3) — by Ito / hepatic stellate cells activated by acetaldehyde & cytokines.
  • Portal inflammation usually mild.

3. Alcoholic Cirrhosis — Late Irreversible Stage

  • Gross — micronodular cirrhosis initially — small uniform nodules (<3 mm), tan-yellow, hard, fibrous; liver size may be normal, enlarged, or shrunken.
  • With time — may evolve into macronodular pattern; mixed micro- & macronodular; pale tan colour, fibrous bands.
  • Microscopy — nodules of regenerating hepatocytes surrounded by dense fibrous septa; bridging fibrosis between central veins & portal tracts; bile duct proliferation; ongoing steatosis & Mallory bodies in some nodules; chronic inflammation in septa.
  • Vascular disturbance — distortion of hepatic architecture → portal hypertension, porto-systemic shunts.

Pathogenesis

  • Alcohol metabolised by alcohol dehydrogenase → acetaldehyde (toxic, forms adducts with tubulin, proteins → Mallory-Denk bodies, impairs secretion of VLDL → triglyceride accumulation → steatosis).
  • MEOS (cytochrome P450 2E1) — generates ROS, oxidises NADPH → oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation.
  • ↑ NADH/NAD+ ratio impairs β-oxidation of fatty acids, favours triglyceride synthesis.
  • Acetaldehyde & ROS activate Kupffer cells & hepatic stellate cells → TGF-β, TNF-α, IL-1, collagen deposition → fibrosis.
  • Gut-derived endotoxin — TLR4 on Kupffer cells → cytokine cascade.
  • Iron overload, oxidative stress, impaired methionine metabolism.

Clinical Pearl

Maddrey discriminant function (4.6 × [PT − control] + bilirubin) >32 predicts severe alcoholic hepatitis with high 28-day mortality — treat with prednisolone (40 mg/day × 28 days) if no contraindication (sepsis, GI bleed, hepatorenal syndrome). Pentoxifylline is alternative. Abstinence is the cornerstone — stops progression and improves survival at any stage.

Thrombocytopenia — Definition & Causes

Thrombocytopenia — platelet count <150,000/μL. Clinical bleeding usually manifest when <50,000; serious / spontaneous bleeding when <20,000; risk of intracranial haemorrhage <10,000.

Causes — Classified by Mechanism

1. Decreased Production

  • Bone marrow failure / infiltration — aplastic anaemia, leukaemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, lymphoma, multiple myeloma, metastatic carcinoma, myelofibrosis.
  • Megakaryocyte-specific injury — drugs (chemotherapy, thiazides, alcohol, oestrogens, valproate, linezolid); radiation; viruses (HIV, HCV, parvovirus B19, EBV, CMV, rubella, mumps, varicella); vitamin B12 / folate deficiency (ineffective thrombopoiesis); iron deficiency (rare).
  • Inherited — Fanconi anaemia, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, May-Hegglin anomaly, Bernard-Soulier syndrome (production defect), amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia (TPO receptor MPL mutation), TAR syndrome (thrombocytopenia-absent radius).
  • Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

2. Increased Destruction

  • Immune-mediated
    • ITP (immune thrombocytopenia) — primary; secondary — SLE, CLL, lymphoma, HIV, HCV, antiphospholipid syndrome; drugs (heparin — HIT, quinine, quinidine, sulfonamides, vancomycin, abciximab); post-transfusion purpura; neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia.
  • Non-immune
    • Microangiopathic — DIC, TTP, HUS, HELLP, malignant hypertension, disseminated malignancy.
    • Mechanical — prosthetic heart valves, extracorporeal circulation, giant haemangioma (Kasabach-Merritt).
    • Infections — malaria, dengue, leptospirosis, severe sepsis, typhoid, scrub typhus.
    • Severe burns, snake bite, massive transfusion (dilutional).

3. Increased Splenic Sequestration / Pooling

  • Splenomegaly — portal hypertension (cirrhosis), congestive splenomegaly, storage diseases (Gaucher, Niemann-Pick), infiltrative (lymphoma, leukaemia), infections (kala-azar, malaria, TB), hypersplenism.
  • Massive transfusion / dilutional — replaces 1.5× blood volume.

4. Pseudothrombocytopenia

  • EDTA-dependent platelet clumping — artefact; check blood smear; collect in citrate tube.
  • Platelet satellitism around neutrophils.
  • Giant platelets excluded by automated counter (Bernard-Soulier, ITP).

Clinical Pearl

Petechiae over lower limbs + mucosal bleeding + normal CBC otherwise → think ITP. Peripheral smear confirms — large platelets, no schistocytes. Initial tests — CBC, smear, LDH, haptoglobin, PT/aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer, ANA, HIV, HCV, HBV, H. pylori, TSH, serum protein electrophoresis; bone marrow biopsy if atypical or refractory. First-line therapy — corticosteroids; IVIG for rapid rise (active bleeding, surgery, pregnancy); TPO-receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim) & rituximab for refractory cases; splenectomy for chronic refractory.
